title: Goodbye to All That
author: Robert Graves
edition_analyzed: Original 1929 edition (notably revised in later editions by the author)
target_audience: Readers interested in World War I history
Those interested in British cultural and social history
core_themes: The horrors and futility of war
The trauma of combat (shell shock, PTSD)
Coming of age and loss of innocence
Social and generational change in early 20th-century Britain
primary_purpose: To chronicle Graves’s experiences in World War I, reflect on their psychological and emotional impacts, and examine how the war severed ties—both personal and cultural—with the pre-war world.

structure_format.narrative_style: Candid, direct, ironic, with elements of dark humor
structure_format.organization: Chronological, beginning with Graves’s childhood and ending with his ‘farewell’ to England, interspersed with vivid war experiences and post-war reflections
features: Critical commentary on British society and the military establishment
Reassessment and revision in later editions

key_concepts_lessons: War profoundly alters individuals and societies, often leaving lasting trauma.
Nostalgia for the pre-war world can obscure structural social problems.
The experience of trench warfare challenges romantic notions of heroism and patriotism.
Survivors often feel alienated both during and after the war.
Personal testimony can counter official narratives and reveal historical truths.
notable_features: One of the earliest and most influential ‘disillusioned’ memoirs of World War I
Candid discussion of mental health and shell shock
Critical look at British society before, during, and after the war
Subject of multiple revisions by Graves himself
cultural_historical_context: Published in the interwar period, ‘Goodbye to All That’ captured a widely-shared sense of loss, trauma, and disillusionment among the so-called ‘lost generation.’ Its frankness and anti-establishment tone broke with prior traditions of war memoir and influenced subsequent war literature, including works by Siegfried Sassoon and Erich Maria Remarque.
reception_impact: Regarded as a seminal work of war literature
Praised for its honesty, literary quality, and influence on public perceptions of World War I
Inspired debate due to Graves’s sometimes unflattering portraits of his contemporaries
Served as a crucial counterpart to official narratives and propaganda
Continues to be widely studied in schools and universities
comparable_titles: Memoirs of an Infantry Officer by Siegfried Sassoon
All Quiet on the Western Front by Erich Maria Remarque
Testament of Youth by Vera Brittain
Undertones of War by Edmund Blunden
